newsitem.title: UK: Insurers must raise standards - UK govt actuary.
newsitem.headline: Insurers must raise standards - UK govt actuary.

text.p: UK insurers can play a major role in relieving the state of the financial burden of long- term care, but only if companies focus more on the customer than on returns to shareholders, the British government actuary said on Tuesday.

"Government in the UK and in many other countries is looking for ways in which the insurance industry can play a part in relieving costs which would cripple government expenditure," British government actuary Chris Daykin told an insurance industry conference.
However, he added that the government would be looking to the insurance industry to help deliver welfare benefits in an atmosphere of flexibility and consumer choice which had often been lacking.
"There are pressures of competition pushing professionalism in the industry into the background," said Daykin.

"Marketing is pushed by the desires of those selling products rather than the customer. Disclosure of information is seen as a burden rather than creating an openness that should be welcomed. And the quality of advice has been mixed, with the pension mis-selling scandal in the UK reflecting a lack of control on marketing and sales," he said.
"The insurance industry has a lot to do," Daykin added.

The comments come in the wake of announcements by the Conservative government in the past week outlining plans to place provision for pensions and long-term care in the hands of the private sector if it wins the forthcoming general election.

Daykin said the Government would have to overcome issues such as ensuring availability to all and preventing any tendency towards discrimination which could create an underclass of people insurance whom companies refuse to underwrite.
There would also have to be some form of security to protect against insurers becoming insolvent and a means of redistribution to people who had not been provided for, he said.
Daykin was speaking at "Insurance and the State", a conference organised in London to mark the centenary of the Chartered Insurance Institute.
